name: Walnut console / sideboard with marble top
description: Hardware-free walnut sideboard: pegged mortise-and-tenon base, housed-dado carcass with floating back, box-jointed drawers, slatted sliding doors in routed tracks, keyed stone top. Auto-exported from the original hand-coded generator (1400 × 400 × 850 mm).
assumptions: Dimensions come from the reference photo proportions, not a measured piece.
steps: Glue the two end frames: legs, end rails and end stretchers
Join the end frames with the front & back aprons and the long stretcher
Set the carcass floor (bottom panel) on the leg tenons
Stand the end panels, divider, drawer rail and guide strips
Slide in the floating back panel
Drop on the carcass roof (top panel)
Lift in the two sliding doors

guide.title: Walnut sideboard with stone top
text: Finished size 1400 × 400 × 850 mm: four legs on an H-stretcher base, a carcass with two drawers and two sliding slatted doors, and a 1400 mm stone top.

No hardware at all. Every connection is glued wood joinery. You will cut six joint families: pegged mortise & tenon, housed dado with tongue, floating-panel grooves, box joints, slat tenons and wooden stone keys.
Build order: base frame → carcass → drawers → sliding doors → top. Dry-fit every joint before glue.
How to read the pictures: orange parts are new in this step; orange boxes inside a part are wood to remove (mortises, dados, grooves); green boxes are tenons and tongues you leave standing.
guide.tip: Cut a spare of every joint type in scrap first. The 20 minutes it costs saves a ruined leg.
guide.chk: Everything in this guide is dimensioned from the same 3D model you can inspect, section and export.

guide.title: Parts overview
text: 26 part types, 89 pieces. Each tile is labelled with its name and quantity; part IDs match the cut list on the next page.
Legs come in a mirror pair (type A ×2, type B ×2) because the stretcher mortise sits on a different face.
The back panel and drawer bottoms are 6 mm veneered ply; everything else is solid walnut except the marble top.
Pegs and stone keys are small offcuts of walnut with the end grain showing.
guide.tip: Label every blank in pencil with its part name and orientation arrow the moment you cut it.

guide.title: Tools & materials
text: Stock: kiln-dried American walnut 8/4 (legs, 56 cm blanks), 5/4 (panels, rails, drawer fronts), 4/4 (everything else); one 6 mm walnut-veneered ply sheet ≥ 1.4 × 0.4 m; one 20 mm marble slab with four blind sockets (ask the fabricator).
Marking: tape measure, steel rule, marking knife, combination square, mortise gauge, marking gauge, pencil.

Cutting: table saw or tenon saw, dozuki saw, bench chisels 6 / 8 / 12 / 25 mm, mallet, shoulder plane, router with straight bits 6, 8, 12 and 18 mm (or router plane + tenon saw), 6 mm drill bit for peg holes.

Gluing & finishing: PVA wood glue, ≥ 8 clamps with cauls, wax or hard-wax oil, 180–320 grit paper, flexible stone adhesive or silicone, felt pads. No screws, nails, brackets, runners, hinges or handles are used.
guide.tip: Let stock acclimatise indoors for a week and mill it oversize first, then to final size just before cutting joints.

guide.title: Anatomy of the main frame joint
text: Every frame joint is a blind mortise & tenon: tenon 8 mm thick (⅓ of the 22 mm rail), 24 mm long (55 % of the 44 mm leg), with shoulders on all four sides.
The mortise stops 15 mm below the leg shoulder so the leg can never split out at the top.
Rails sit 4 mm back from the leg faces for a clean shadow line.
A 6 × 6 mm square peg locks each joint. When you drill the tenon, offset its hole 1.5 mm toward the shoulder (draw-boring): the peg pulls the joint tight without clamps.
guide.tip: Orange pieces here show how parts slide apart. In the build they glue together.
guide.chk: Tenon should enter the mortise with light hand pressure and no rocking.

guide.title: Mark out the legs
text: Plane four legs to 44 × 44 × 580 mm (20 mm extra on top for the tenon and trimming). Choose the best two adjacent faces as the outside faces.
Pair them: two type A (front-left and back-right) and two type B (front-right and back-left). Type B has its stretcher mortise on the other inside face, so mark it as a mirror image.
With a square and knife, mark the shoulder line 560 mm from the foot. Everything is measured from the outside faces.

Set the mortise gauge to 8 mm, 11 mm from the outside face; mark mortise A and B (24 × 40 mm each, top edge 15 mm below the shoulder). Mark the stretcher mortise (24 × 20, thickness 10 mm) centred at 202 mm.
guide.tip: Mark both leg types at the same time from one story stick so heights match to the millimetre.
guide.chk: Hold type A and B back-to-back: the marks should mirror each other.

guide.title: Chop the rail mortises (A and B)
text: Clamp the leg on the bench. Drill out most of the waste with a 8 mm brad-point bit stopped at 24 mm (tape flag on the bit).
Chop the remainder with the 8 mm chisel, working from the centre toward each end; keep the chisel vertical and leave ~1 mm to the knife line.
Pare the walls and end walls to the line, flat and square. Mortise A (24 × 8 × 40) and B are the same size, on the two inside faces.
Cheek rule: the wall on the outside is 11 mm, more than the 8 mm tenon, so it will not blow out.
guide.tip: Cut mortise B first, then A: the two meet inside the leg corner but never touch because their tenons stop 4 mm short of each other.
guide.chk: Slide the shank of an 8 mm drill bit in: it should sit square to the face all the way down.

guide.title: Stretcher mortise and peg holes
text: Chop the stretcher mortise 24 mm deep, 10 mm thick, 20 mm tall on the inside face (type A: toward the other leg of the same end; type B: the other face).
Chisel or drill the peg holes 6 × 6 mm: two apron holes 22 mm deep from each outside face, and one stretcher hole 30 mm deep.
Square holes: drive a sharp 6 mm chisel across the grain, then pare. You may drill Ø6 round holes and use round pegs instead.
Break every edge lightly with 240-grit paper.
guide.tip: Peg holes go through the leg cheek and stop inside the far wall: never through the leg.
guide.chk: Blind holes: the peg stands flush with the outside face when fully driven.

guide.title: Cut the top tenon on every leg
text: Square off the top to the 560 mm shoulder. Mark a 24 × 24 mm tenon, 14 mm tall, centred, leaving a 10 mm shoulder on all sides.
Saw the cheeks, then the shoulders, and pare them clean with the shoulder plane.
These four tenons locate the carcass floor and hold it in place with glue.
guide.tip: Cut the top tenons after the mortises so the legs stay long and easy to hold while chopping.
guide.chk: Tenon should push into a test mortise in scrap with a gentle tap.

guide.title: Cut the apron-rail tenons
text: Rails: 22 × 60 mm; front/back 1340 mm long, end rails 340 mm long (finished sizes include 24 mm tenons).
Gauge the tenon 8 mm thick, 7 mm from the inside face of the rail. Mark it 40 mm tall: 5 mm shoulder below, 15 mm above.
Saw the cheeks to the line, then the shoulders. Pare cheeks flat; trim until it enters the mortise with light hand pressure.
Drill/chisel the tenon peg hole 12 mm from the shoulder. For draw-boring, shift it 1.5 mm toward the shoulder from the leg hole centre.
guide.tip: Cut all eight tenons from one set-up on the saw so they are identical.
guide.chk: Test each tenon in its own leg; mark the pair with a matching number.

guide.title: Stretcher tenons and the long-stretcher mortise
text: End stretchers: 30 × 30 × 340 mm. Tenons 10 mm thick, 20 tall, 24 long, centred; peg hole 12 mm from each shoulder.
Chop the central mortise (22 deep × 10 wide × 20 tall) on the inside face of each end stretcher, exactly at mid-length.
Long stretcher: 30 × 30 × 1350 mm with a 10 × 20 × 22 mm tenon at each end.
This is the H of the H-stretcher: two ends joined by the long one at mid-depth.
guide.tip: Cut both end stretchers together, clamped face-to-face, for matching mortises.
guide.chk: Test-fit the long stretcher between the two end stretchers: no gaps at the shoulders.

guide.title: Glue the two end frames
text: Dry-fit first: each end frame is two legs + one end rail + one end stretcher.
Brush glue on the mortise walls only (not the tenon, so squeeze-out stays outside). Push all tenons home.
Clamp across the shoulders. Check both frames for twist by sighting across them; adjust clamps until flat.
Check the diagonals of each end frame: they must match within 1 mm.
guide.tip: Leave the pegs out for now. Glue the end frames as a mirror pair on a flat surface.
guide.chk: Wipe squeeze-out off with a damp rag before it skins.

guide.title: Join the end frames
text: Stand the two end frames up and slide in the front and back aprons and the long stretcher together.
Glue every mortise. Seat the long stretcher into the end stretchers first, then the aprons.
Clamp across the width at the apron and stretcher heights; check the base sits on a flat floor without rocking.
guide.tip: Measure diagonals across the top of the legs: equal diagonals = square frame.
guide.chk: Frame sits flat; the four top shoulders are level (tape-measure from a table).

guide.title: Drive the draw-bore pegs
text: Taper the tip of each 6 × 6 mm peg with a knife (a short wedge point).
Drive the apron pegs (22 mm) and stretcher pegs (30 mm) from the outside faces, tapping with the mallet. Because the tenon hole is offset, each peg draws the shoulder tight.
Leave pegs 1 mm proud; trim and pare flush after the glue is dry.
12 pegs total: 8 at the aprons, 4 at the stretchers.
guide.tip: Drive pegs with the grain of the leg running the same way as the peg grain to avoid splitting.
guide.chk: No peg should bend or crack. If it does, enlarge the offset less next time (1.5 mm max).

guide.title: Bottom panel: mortises, dados and tracks
text: Glue up boards to 1380 × 380 × 22 mm. Flatten and sand the top face.
Chop four 24 × 24 × 14 mm blind mortises in the underside for the leg tenons.
Router (or plane) 18 × 8 mm dados on the top face for the end panels (at 8 mm from each end) and the divider. All stop 14 mm from the front edge.
Rout the 6 mm back groove (6 deep) 20 mm from the rear edge and the two 18 × 5 mm door tracks from the divider to the right end panel.
guide.tip: Clamp a straight-edge fence to guide the router for every dado: set the fence once for each width.
guide.chk: Dry-fit an end-panel tongue in its dado: snug, not tight.

guide.title: Top panel: dados, tracks and key mortises
text: Same size as the bottom: 1380 × 380 × 22 mm. Work on the underside: the dados mirror the bottom panel (8 mm deep).
Door tracks are 12 mm deep here (5 mm in the bottom): this extra depth lets you lift each door in, then drop it down.
Rout the 6 mm back groove (6 deep).
On the top face chop four 12 × 12 × 8 mm key mortises. Keep them away from the door tracks.
guide.tip: Rout the 12 mm tracks in two passes of 6 mm.
guide.chk: The 2 mm web between track and key mortise must stay intact.

guide.title: End panels
text: Two panels 18 × 380 × 226 mm. Cut an 8 mm tongue top and bottom (stopped 14 mm from the front).
Both panels: 6 × 6 mm back groove on the inside face, 20 mm from the rear edge.
Left panel only (drawer side): one 20 × 6 mm dado for the drawer rail and two 10 × 4 mm stopped dados for the drawer guide strips.
Mark L and R on the inside faces: the grooves are a mirror pair.
guide.tip: Cut the tongues first so you can use the same fence setting for both panels.
guide.chk: Place L and R face to face: their back grooves should line up.

guide.title: Divider, drawer rail and guide strips
text: Divider: 18 mm thick, tongued top and bottom like the end panels. On its left face cut the same rail dado (20 × 6) and two strip dados (10 × 4).
Drawer rail: 20 mm tall; a 6 mm long tongue on each end (stopped 10 mm from the front) fits the rail dados.
Guide strips (×4): 10 × 10 mm. The first 4 mm of the thickness glues into the dado; the other 6 mm slides in the drawer groove. Wax them.
guide.tip: Make the four strips from one length of straight-grain stock and crosscut after planing.
guide.chk: The strip should seat in its dado with finger pressure and protrude exactly 6 mm.

guide.title: Floating back panel
text: Cut the 6 mm ply to 1340 × 238 mm. It floats in the 6 mm grooves of the top, bottom and end panels.
Notch the four corners 6 × 6 mm so the panel clears the dado shoulders.
Never glue it. A loose panel lets the solid wood move with the seasons.
Finish the inside face before assembly.
guide.tip: Sand a 1 mm chamfer on the edges so it slides easily into the grooves.
guide.chk: It slips into the groove with 0.5 mm of play at each end.

guide.title: Set the carcass floor on the base
text: Glue only the four leg tenons and set the bottom panel onto them.
Keep the panel flush with the outside faces of the legs and 2 mm back from the front line of the aprons.
Weight the panel overnight with sandbags; no clamps needed.
guide.tip: The aprons carry the load; the tenons just locate and hold.
guide.chk: Panel overhangs the legs by 0: the legs are flush with the carcass edges.

guide.title: Stand the bay walls
text: Dry-fit the order: glue the drawer rail into the left end panel and divider first, with the guide strips glued in their dados.
Spread glue in the stopped dados of the bottom panel and stand the left end panel, divider and right end panel upright.
Check the drawer opening is square and exactly 470 mm wide (a spacer stick helps).
guide.tip: Keep the strip dado walls free of glue squeeze-out; wax them after.
guide.chk: Drawer rail is level; strips are parallel to the carcass sides.

guide.title: Slide in the back panel
text: Slide the floating back panel down the end-panel grooves and into the bottom groove from the rear.
Do not glue it. The panel must stay free to move.
Check it is straight; the rear 14 mm lip of the panels protects the panel edges.
guide.tip: Wax the groove walls so it slides without sticking.

guide.title: Fit the top panel
text: Spread glue in the end-panel and divider dados in the top panel, then lower it over the tongues.
Clamp across the carcass at the front and back; check square with diagonals.
Wipe off squeeze-out inside the drawer and door bays now. It is almost impossible to reach later.
guide.tip: Pre-assemble dry with the clamps to find any binding before applying glue.
guide.chk: Door tracks above and below are in line when you sight along them.

guide.title: Drawer: box joints
text: Each drawer: front 22 × 100 × 467 mm, sides 12 × 100 × 355 mm. Front/side joint is a 5-finger box joint, 20 mm fingers.
Mark the side's front end with the finger grid; the side gets notches at 0-2-4, the front's ends get fingers at 0-2-4.
Cut on the table saw with a box-joint jig, or by hand: knife, saw the walls, chop the waste with a 12 mm chisel.
Cut the rear joints between sides and back the same way, but only above the bottom groove (from 14 mm up).
guide.tip: Make the first joint 0.1 mm tight and plane to fit; a loose box joint cannot be fixed.
guide.chk: Fingers should push in under hand pressure and finish flush on both faces.

guide.title: Drawer: grooves and finger pull
text: Router a 6 mm groove, 8 mm deep, 8 mm up from the bottom edge across the inside of the front, and 5 mm deep along the inside of each side (open at the rear so the bottom slides in).
On the outside of each side rout the 12 mm tall × 5.5 mm deep runner groove at mid-height, from 22 mm behind the front to the rear end.
On the front face, cut the finger pull 120 × 20 mm, 12 mm deep, near the top edge.
The drawer bottom is 6 mm ply, loose in the grooves.
guide.tip: Rout the runner groove before gluing the drawer. It is a thousand times easier.
guide.chk: A guide strip dropped in the runner groove has about 1 mm of play.

guide.title: Glue up a drawer
text: Dry-fit: slide the bottom into the front groove and the two side grooves from the rear, then add the back.
Glue only the box joints. The bottom stays loose.
Clamp across the front and back; check the drawer is square by diagonals (equal within 1 mm).
Let it set flat on a bench.
guide.tip: Do not glue the bottom: it needs to float.
guide.chk: Drawer sits flat on the bench with no rock.

guide.title: Fit the drawers
text: Wax the guide strips and the drawer runner grooves with paraffin or candle wax.
Slide each drawer in from the front: the groove picks up the strip.
Plane the sides until there is a 1.5 mm gap each side and 1.5 mm above and below.
guide.tip: Mark which drawer goes where (L-lower, U-upper) on the underside.
guide.chk: Drawer front is flush with the carcass front, within 1 mm.

guide.title: Door stiles and rails
text: Each door is 440 × 233 × 16 mm: two 24 × 16 stiles and two 30 × 16 rails.
Chop 18 × 5 × 20 mm mortises at both ends of each stile; saw matching tenons on the rails.
On the rails cut 16 slat mortises 8 × 5 × 12 mm at 23.8 mm pitch (gap 11.8 mm).
Door height 233 mm = opening + 7 mm: that is what lets you lift it into the deep top track and drop it into the bottom one.
guide.tip: Use a story stick for the slat spacing and mark both rails together.
guide.chk: Both rails must have identical mortise positions.

guide.title: Slats
text: Plane 32 slats to 12 × 16 mm, 197 mm long including tenons.
Cut an 8 × 5 × 12 mm tenon on both ends. A stop block on the saw makes every slat identical.
Ease the long edges with 240-grit; a very slight chamfer catches the light.
guide.tip: Cut one spare slat per door.
guide.chk: Shoulder-to-shoulder length must be identical: check with a stop block.

guide.title: Glue up a door
text: Dry-fit the slats into the bottom rail, then add the top rail.
Glue the slat tenons into the rails first, then add the stiles. Clamp across the rails only.
Check square and flat on a bench; wipe any squeeze-out.
Make two doors: they are identical.
guide.tip: Use a spacer strip between slats during glue-up.
guide.chk: Slats parallel and all spaced equally.

guide.title: Install the doors
text: Wax both tracks and the top and bottom edges of the doors.
Lift the door up into the 12 mm top track until the bottom clears, swing the bottom in over its 5 mm track, then drop it down.
Door A (left) in the front track, door B (right) in the rear track. They pass each other with a 6 mm web between them.
Plane the stile edge until the door slides freely but without rattling.
guide.tip: If the door binds, wax first. Then plane no more than 0.2 mm at a time.
guide.chk: Each door slides the full opening without touching the other door.

guide.title: Stone keys and sockets
text: The stone has four 12 × 12 × 6 mm blind sockets in its underside; the fabricator drills them from your drawing.
Each walnut key (12 × 12 × 14 mm) sits 8 mm in the top-panel mortise and 6 mm in the stone socket.
Glue the keys only into the wood mortises. The stone sockets get a drop of silicone so the stone can lift off for service.
guide.tip: Dry-fit the stone first; never test-fit with glue on.
guide.chk: Stone sits on the top panel without rocking; sockets line up.

guide.title: Fit the stone keys
text: Glue the four keys into the top-panel mortises, end grain up.
Wipe off any glue; let it cure 30 minutes.
guide.tip: Mark the key positions on the underside of the stone with tape to find them quickly.

guide.title: Bed the marble top
text: Run a thin zig-zag of flexible stone adhesive on the top panel (not near the edges).
Lower the stone vertically onto the keys with two people; check the 10 mm overhang is even.
Weight with sandbags 24 h.
guide.tip: Protect the stone edge with a towel while lifting.
guide.chk: Overhang: 10 mm all round (check at four points).

guide.title: Finish and enjoy
text: Sand to 240 grit, remove dust, then apply two coats of hard-wax oil. Do not oil the stone.
Fit felt pads under the feet if the floor needs them.
Check once a year: wax the door tracks and drawer strips.
You built it with no hardware.
guide.tip: Give the first coat of oil 24 hours before the second.
